"So I'm looking at that as a really good sign." Spencer said Fawcett, her family and friends are clinging to hope for a recovery. "She [Alana Stewart] doesn't want to throw out a number. And neither does Farrah. ... They're still hoping for that miracle," Spencer said. "Farrah's Story," a documentary-style program that has followed the course of her illness and showed her grueling treatment in graphic detail, aired on NBC Friday and was viewed by almost 9 million people. Fawcett and partner Ryan O'Neal watched the show together, Spencer confirmed. "Alana said it was the ultimate in bittersweet," Spencer said. "You know, they're reliving two years of hell that they've endured together." King asked Spencer whether Fawcett, who made her name a household word on the hit '70s TV series "Charlie's Angels," and O'Neal might marry. "He said you never know. He was cagey about it," Spencer said. "And, you know, I think he would in a second. He's so madly in love with her." King also had a panel of medical experts on his show to discuss Fawcett's cancer. Dr. Thomas Vogl, who at one time treated the actress in Germany, called her medical condition "very, very serious." Dr. Allyson Ocean, a medical oncologist in New York, said only about 5,000 cases of anal cancer are diagnosed in the United States yearly. Unlike Fawcett's case, it usually doesn't spread, and only about 10 to 15 percent of cases are advanced, Ocean said. Fawcett's cancer, however, is in Stage 4 and has spread to her liver. Ocean said there are various causes of anal cancer. "One of the causes is a virus called the human papilloma virus, which is a sexually transmitted virus. It seems to be more common in women, in general, outside of any viral infections. Smoking is actually a risk factor," she said. King asked Dr. Paul Song, a radiation oncologist, if he had seen Stage 4 cancer cured. "Not with anal cancer. I have seen it with other GI malignancies such as rectal cancer," Song said. "But anal cancer is a little bit more difficult to treat." Despite the bleak outlook, Song had praise for Fawcett and her documentary. "I think one of the most powerful things that Miss Fawcett did in this documentary was give patients a sense of hope and to just show how she's handled this with such courage and dignity," Song said. CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta told King that doctors have to strike a delicate balance when they are caring for patients such as Fawcett. "You have to be absolutely honest with patients, but, you know, you don't want to strip away their hope and optimism, either. There are people, Larry, as you know, who beat the odds," Gupta said. Vogl told King he developed a close relationship with Fawcett during the time he treated her in Germany and expressed admiration for his one-time patient. "From a lot of treatments and contact and communication, I think she is extremely special, an extremely brave person," he said.

Fawcett was first diagnosed with anal cancer in September 2006. While many public figures in her position might have retreated behind private gates or used vague language to describe their illness, Fawcett made a conscious decision to go public. 

Anal cancer, which affects roughly 5,000 Americans a year, carries an unfortunate social stigma due to its location and association with certain strains of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV). Because of this, it is rarely discussed openly in mainstream media. Fawcett’s diagnosis shattered that silence.

After undergoing aggressive chemotherapy and radiation, Fawcett was initially declared cancer-free in early 2007. However, during a routine checkup just four months later, doctors discovered the cancer had returned and metastasized to her liver. 

Faced with a devastating prognosis, Fawcett turned the camera on herself.

### Unfiltered and Unvarnished: *Farrah's Story*

Shot primarily on handheld camcorders by Fawcett and her close friend, Alana Stewart, *Farrah’s Story* was never meant to be a polished Hollywood production. Instead, the two-hour NBC special captured the visceral reality of living with terminal cancer. 

Viewers watched as Fawcett endured painful procedures, suffered from violent nausea, traveled to Germany for alternative cutting-edge therapies, and eventually shaved off her famed blonde locks when chemotherapy caused them to fall out. 

"Cancer is a disease that is mysterious, stubborn, and cruel," Fawcett said in a voiceover during the special. "I hold onto the hope that there is some reason I'm going through this."

The documentary did not shy away from the excruciating moments: Fawcett weeping in pain on a hospital bed, her longtime partner Ryan O’Neal holding her hand as she drifted in and out of consciousness, and her anguish over her son, Redmond O'Neal, who visited her in hospital garb while serving time in prison on drug charges.

The reaction to *Farrah’s Story* was swift and overwhelmingly emotional. Television critics, while noting the difficult and painful nature of the footage, praised Fawcett for her extraordinary courage.

*The New York Times* described the film as "an unusually raw portrait of illness," noting that Fawcett "sacrificed her privacy to demystify a disease." *USA Today* called it "a heartbreaking, heroic document of human endurance."

While *Farrah’s Story* was met with immense empathy, it was also framed by an inescapable sense of tragedy. By the time the documentary aired in May 2009, Fawcett was bedridden in a Los Angeles hospital, her body weakened by years of relentless treatment.

Fawcett was first diagnosed with anal cancer in September 2006. After undergoing aggressive chemotherapy and radiation, she was initially declared cancer-free on her 60th birthday in February 2007. Just months later, however, a routine checkup revealed the disease had returned and metastasized to her liver. 

Rather than retreating into privacy, Fawcett made the brave decision to open up her fight to the world, allowing cameras to document her treatments, her pain, and her relentless hope. 

### A Taboo Diagnosis and a Profile in Courage

When Fawcett was diagnosed, the specific nature of her illness—anal cancer—carried a societal stigma that often forced patients into silence. Fawcett refused to hide. 

"Anal cancer carries an unfair and devastating stigma, largely because people are uncomfortable discussing that part of the body," said CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta. "By being open about her diagnosis, Farrah did something extraordinary. She stripped away the shame and turned a deeply personal tragedy into a public health learning moment. Clinically, treating recurrent stage IV cancer that has spread to the liver is an immense uphill battle, but her willingness to pursue every option—from standard therapies to innovative treatments abroad—showed a patient taking complete agency over her fight."

Seeking advanced options, Fawcett traveled to Germany multiple times for specialized treatments, including targeted chemoembolization and alternative stem-cell therapies not yet approved in the United States. 

Dr. Lawrence Piro, Fawcett’s chief oncologist in Los Angeles, recalled her tenacity during these exhausting medical journeys. 

"Farrah was an extraordinarily knowledgeable and engaged patient," Dr. Piro noted. "She didn't just accept a prognosis; she interrogated it. She read the research, asked tough questions, and fought with every ounce of her strength. She approached her treatment not as a victim, but as a warrior looking for the next strategy."

### Captivating Hollywood and Redefining the Celebrity Narrative

For those in the entertainment industry, watching one of Hollywood's most beautiful icons face a debilitating disease with such raw honesty was deeply moving. 

Lara Spencer, veteran entertainment journalist and television host, reflected on the profound shift in how the public viewed Fawcett during this time.

"Farrah was the golden girl—the woman every man wanted to be with and every woman wanted to be," Spencer said. "When she got sick, she could have pulled the curtains closed. Instead, she invited us in. She showed herself without makeup, without her famous hair, wracked with pain in a hospital bed. It was terrifyingly real, but it was also the bravest thing a celebrity of her stature could do. Farrah proved that true beauty isn't about red carpets or photo shoots; it’s about resilience."

Spencer added that Fawcett's willingness to document her fight fundamentally changed how Hollywood approaches serious illness. "She broke the unspoken rule that stars had to remain picture-perfect at all costs. She showed us that it's okay to be vulnerable, and in doing so, she gave strength to millions of everyday people fighting the exact same battle in the dark."

### The Legacy of 'Farrah's Story'

Fawcett’s fight culminated in the televised documentary *Farrah’s Story*, which she shot largely herself alongside her close friend Alana Stewart. The footage was raw, showing the agonizing side effects of chemotherapy, the emotional toll on her longtime partner Ryan O'Neal, and the fleeting moments of joy and comfort she found along the way.

When the documentary aired, it drew over 9 million viewers, earning an Emmy nomination and sparking a nationwide conversation about cancer care, patient advocacy, and end-of-life dignity.

Medical experts agree that her impact extended far beyond the screen. 

"When a high-profile figure shines a light on a rare or stigmatized illness, the ripple effect in the medical community is profound," said Dr. Elizabeth Walsh, a surgical oncologist specializing in gastrointestinal cancers. "We saw a noticeable increase in patients seeking early screenings and asking informed questions. Farrah Fawcett undoubtedly saved lives by demystifying the disease and encouraging early intervention."

### An Enduring Symbol of Hope

Throughout her ordeal, Fawcett established the Farrah Fawcett Foundation, dedicated to funding cutting-edge cancer research, prevention, and patient assistance funds for those in need. 

While her physical prognosis grew increasingly dire in the spring of 2009, those close to her and the medical professionals who treated her maintained that her spirit remained unbroken. 

"Her body was fighting a losing battle, but her spirit never lost," Dr. Gupta remarked. "In medicine, we look at courage not just by how long a patient survives, but by how they choose to live the time they have left. Farrah Fawcett lived those final years with immense grace, advocacy, and purpose."

Farrah Fawcett passed away on June 25, 2009, at the age of 62. Yet, decades after she first captivated the world as a poster girl, she is remembered not just for how she lived in the spotlight, but for the courage, dignity, and light she brought to the darkness of a devastating disease.

On *Larry King Live*, particularly during segments broadcast in May and June 2009 around the release of the NBC documentary *Farrah’s Story* and her subsequent passing, Larry King hosted extensive discussions about Farrah Fawcett’s battle with cancer. 

Key figures featured in these broadcasts included her longtime partner **Ryan O’Neal**, her close friend and documentary co-producer **Alana Stewart**, her chief US oncologist **Dr. Lawrence Piro**, and CNN medical experts like **Dr. Sanjay Gupta**.

The discussions focused on three main areas: the documentary itself, her oncologist's perspective on her timeline/prognosis, and the grim medical statistics surrounding Stage 4 anal cancer.

---

### 1. The Documentary (*Farrah’s Story*)
* **Origins and Purpose:** Alana Stewart and Ryan O'Neal explained that the project began as simple home videos intended to document Fawcett's journey for her own review. It evolved into a documentary when Fawcett realized her story could inspire others fighting cancer, destigmatize the disease, and shed light on alternative treatments.
* **Unfiltered Reality:** The show highlighted how raw the footage was. It showed Fawcett in agonizing pain, suffering from severe side effects (vomiting, hair loss, extreme fatigue), undergoing blood transfusions, and facing the psychological toll of her condition.
* **Privacy Infringement:** A major point of discussion on *Larry King Live* was Fawcett’s crusade against medical privacy violations. The documentary exposed that UCLA Medical Center employees had illegally accessed and leaked her confidential medical records to tabloids before she even had time to process bad news herself.

---

### 2. Her Doctor’s Timetable and Prognosis
Dr. Lawrence Piro, Fawcett's primary oncologist at St. John's Health Center in Santa Monica, appeared on the show to discuss her medical journey, treatment choices, and timeline:

* **Initial Remission to Recurrence:** Dr. Piro noted that after her initial diagnosis in late 2006, Fawcett underwent aggressive chemotherapy and radiation, which temporarily put her into remission. However, during a routine checkup in May 2007, doctors discovered the cancer had returned and metastasized to her liver.
* **Refusing a "Expiration Date":** Dr. Piro discussed how traditional medical statistics suggested a very short survival window once anal cancer metastasizes to the liver (often less than a year). However, Fawcett refused to accept a definitive "timetable" or "death sentence." 
* **Extending the Timeline:** Dr. Piro explained that her fight lasted much longer than typical expectations for Stage 4 metastatic anal cancer. Her decision to seek innovative treatments in Germany (such as chemoembolization—injecting chemo directly into liver tumors—and stem cell therapy) was credited with extending her life by nearly two years beyond her initial recurrence.
* **The Final Phase:** By April 2009, Dr. Piro revealed that the treatments were no longer holding back the disease, and her body was beginning to succumb to liver failure and infectious complications, leading to her hospitalization and death in June 2009.

---

### 3. Medical Statistics on Stage 4 Anal Cancer
During these broadcasts, medical experts on the show (including Dr. Piro and Dr. Sanjay Gupta) broke down the harsh reality of anal cancer and why Fawcett’s fight was so difficult:

* **Rarity:** Anal cancer is a relatively rare form of gastrointestinal cancer (accounting for only about 1–2% of all gut-related cancers at the time). Because it is rare, there were far fewer clinical trials, funding dollars, and standardized FDA-approved treatment protocols compared to breast, lung, or colon cancers.
* **Stage 4 Survival Rates:** Medical statistics presented on the show indicated that for localized (Stage 1 or 2) anal cancer, the 5-year survival rate was relatively high (around 70–80%). However, for **Stage 4 anal cancer**—where the disease has spread to distant organs like the liver—the 5-year survival rate dropped dramatically to **approximately 10% to 15%**.
* **Liver Metastasis:** Experts pointed out that once anal cancer spreads to the liver, complete eradication is virtually impossible with standard surgery or radiation. The primary goal shifts from a cure to palliative care, disease suppression, and extending life span—which made Fawcett’s two-year survival after her liver metastasis noteworthy.
* **Stigma and HPV:** The show addressed the social stigma associated with anal cancer, noting that it is frequently caused by Human Papillomavirus (HPV). Dr. Gupta and Larry King emphasized that Fawcett’s willingness to be public about a "taboo" disease helped break down shame, encouraging people to get screened and talk to their doctors.
